items.label: section_header
items.text: THE TEST FOR UNSATURATED COMPOUNDS

items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: You must be careful with the words you use here: the final mixture is colourless and not clear. Do not use the word clear. Clear means not cloudy, you can see through it. The bromine water is clear and any other solution can also be described as clear.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 25.3 The result of shaking a liquid alkene (left) or alkane (right) with bromine water.

items.label: section_header
items.text: EXTENSION WORK

items.label: text
items.text: In Figure 25.3, interestingly, most of the colour in the right-hand tube is now in the top organic layer. That is because the covalent bromine, which has a simple molecular structure, is more soluble in the organic compound than it is in water.

items.label: section_header
items.text: THE ADDITION OF BROMINE

items.label: text
items.text: Bromine adds to alkenes without any need for heat, light or a catalyst. The reaction is often carried out using bromine water (aqueous bromine solution) as, for example, in Figure 25.2, with ethene.

items.label: text
items.text: You know a reaction has happened because bromine water is orange but the product, called 1,2-dibromoethane, is a colourless liquid.

items.label: text
items.text: You can write this as an equation in two ways: first, using displayed formulae and second, using structural formulae.

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 25.2 An addition reaction: an alkene plus bromine

items.label: text
items.text: Any compound with a carbon-carbon double bond will react with bromine in a similar way to ethene. This is used to test for a carbon-carbon double bond. If you shake an unknown organic compound with bromine water and the orange bromine water is decolourised (the colour changes from orange to colourless), the compound contains a carbon-carbon double bond. If your unknown compound is a gas, you can simply bubble it through bromine water with the same effect.

items.label: text
items.text: The left-hand tube in Figure 25.3 shows the effect of shaking a liquid alkene with bromine water. The organic layer (containing the alkene) is on top. You can see that the bromine water has been completely decolourised, showing the presence of the carbon-carbon double bond.

items.label: text
items.text: The right-hand tube in Figure 25.3 shows what happens if you use a liquid alkane, which doesn't have a carbon-carbon double bond. The colour of the bromine is still there. Alkanes do not decolourise bromine water because they do not contain a carbon-carbon double bond.

items.label: text
items.text: The addition reaction between bromine and propene is very similar to that of ethene. Part of the carbon-carbon double bond breaks and two bromine atoms add across the bond, as shown in Figure 25.4.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 25.4 An addition reaction of propene with bromine

items.label: text
items.text: The product is called 1,2-dibromopropane. Its structure is based on propane and the prefix '1,2-dibromo' shows there are two bromine atoms, on the first and the second carbon atoms.
